analysis.one_liner: Creates government-seeded personal retirement investment accounts with tax-deductible contributions and annuity payouts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in June 2001, sent to its Social Security Subcommittee, and died there when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new 'Individual Retirement Investment Program' alongside Social Security. Every person born on or after July 1, 2002 would get a personal investment account seeded with $1,000 from the Treasury, and anyone could add up to $5,000 a year per account as a tax-deductible contribution. The money would be invested in government securities, bonds, certificates of deposit, insurance contracts, or a broad stock-market index fund, chosen by a federal board; account holders would sign a form acknowledging the government does not protect them from losses. At retirement, monthly benefits would be paid first out of the account balance, and the rest would be paid out as annuities bought from private insurers or rolled into other retirement plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Newborns would each get a $1,000 government-funded account. Households that can afford to contribute up to $5,000 a year per account would get an above-the-line income tax deduction for it — a benefit worth most to people who actually owe income tax. Life insurers would gain a steady stream of customers, since retiring account holders would use their balances to buy annuity contracts from private companies. Asset managers would manage the fixed-income side of the fund.

how_it_helps.text: Each person born on or after July 1, 2002 would get a personal investment account seeded with a $1,000 initial contribution from the Treasury's general fund [S3].
Individuals could contribute up to $5,000 per year per account (a $10,000 annual cap on total contributions) and deduct the full amount from income taxes, even without itemizing [S3].

Account balances would earn whatever the underlying investments earn, credited pro rata to each account, and contributions would be nonforfeitable and held in trust exclusively for the account holder [S3].

Account holders could choose among a government securities fund, a fixed-income fund, and a common-stock index fund designed to mirror the whole U.S. equity market, with the federal Thrift-style board required to seek low administrative costs [S3].
The bill includes spousal consent rules, survivor annuity defaults, and recognition of divorce court orders and child-support and child-abuse judgments against account balances [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury's general fund would pay the $1,000 seed for every newborn and lose revenue from the new deductions. Account holders would bear the investment risk themselves — the bill requires them to sign an acknowledgment that the government does not guarantee any return or protect against loss. Retirees would bear the pricing of annuity contracts purchased from private insurers, and part of their guaranteed Social Security benefit would effectively be paid out of their own account balance first.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, account holders, and future retirees

drawbacks.text: Investing in the fixed-income or stock funds would be explicitly at the account holder's own risk, with no government protection against loss [S3].

The tax deduction for contributions would deliver its largest dollar benefits to households with the income to contribute $5,000 a year and a tax bill to shelter, while the Treasury pays every newborn's $1,000 seed up front [S3].

Monthly retirement benefits would be paid first out of the account holder's personal balance, shifting part of the guaranteed benefit onto money the individual and the government put into the account [S3].

At retirement, account balances would have to be converted into annuity contracts purchased from private companies, routing payouts through insurers' margins rather than direct government payment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The $1,000 seed accounts are a real, if modest, benefit that reaches everyone. But the larger dollar benefits — the tax-deductible contributions — flow mainly to households wealthy enough to contribute and owe taxes, and the design shifts investment risk onto individuals and routes retirement payouts through private insurers. Congress never weighed these trade-offs: the bill died in a subcommittee without a hearing, a debate, or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security Subcommittee and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Petri introduced the bill on June 7, 2001, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1] [S5].
On June 20, 2001, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Social Security, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
Only one House Democrat cosponsored the bill, and no version was ever reported out of committee, debated, or voted on before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill dead, the Treasury kept the money it would have spent on $1,000 seed contributions and lost no revenue to the new deductions, Social Security's benefit structure stayed as it was, and private insurers did not gain the mandated annuity business it would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and high earners missed a windfall

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over Social Security and tax policy
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Social Security and never scheduled a markup or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican with a single Democratic cosponsor; the bill never advanced far enough for any vote that would show a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would make private annuity sellers the mandatory channel for retirement payouts: retiring account holders' balances would be spent buying annuity contracts from companies in the business of selling annuities, and the fixed-income fund would also invest in insurance contracts. Insurers would gain a built-in customer base, subject to bonding and contract-term requirements.

Fixed-income investments in the trust fund would be selected by qualified professional asset managers, giving the industry a new government-funded client. The stock portion would be a centrally managed index fund with no individual stock picking, limiting the industry's role and fees.

The up-to-$5,000-per-year deductible contribution is worth the most to families able to contribute regularly and shelter income, while the financing — the $1,000 seed for every newborn — comes from the general fund that all taxpayers support.
